plan.factor: Silicon-to-aluminium ratio of the gel, Si/(Al + small constant)
queries: product Si/Al ranges reported for FAU and LTA syntheses versus ZSM-5 (MFI) syntheses
how gel Si/Al ratio controls framework selection low-silica FAU LTA versus high-silica MFI BEA
plan.why: Si/Al is the single most framework-discriminating synthesis variable in zeolite synthesis: low Si/Al gels (rich in alkali) give low-silica frameworks like FAU, LTA, SOD and MOR, while high Si/Al (often fluoride or OSDA-dominated media) gives high-silica frameworks like MFI, MTW, *BEA and TON, and Si/Al near zero selects aluminophosphates (AFI, AEL, AEI). The classifier receives Si and Al only as separate normalized mole fractions, and a tree ensemble splits on one column at a time, so it cannot directly express the ratio; the same Si mole fraction with a 10x different Al level lands in different leaves. Encoding the ratio makes this boundary axis directly splittable and transfers across publications, unlike paper-specific absolute gel concentrations.

descriptor.assumptions: Si and Al mole fractions of the normalized gel are taken as a faithful proxy for the reactive (dissolved) Si/Al ratio, ignoring speciation, Al from the source (e.g. seeds or impurities), and the fact that P may replace Si as the tetrahedral framework former in aluminophosphate chemistry (in that regime Si/Al alone is not the driver; a follow-up P/Al or Si+P/(Al) ratio may be needed). The constant 0.001 only guards against division by zero and caps the ratio at ~Si/0.001; a tree can still rank these capped values by Si. Heteroatom substitution (B, Ga, Ge, Zn, Ti) is ignored here and would be covered by later descriptors.
descriptor.expected_effect: As gel_si_al_ratio increases from ~0: aluminophosphate outcomes (AFI, AEL, AEI) dominate when Si is absent relative to Al+P; at low ratios (~1-5) low-silica frameworks FAU, LTA, SOD and low-silica MOR are favoured; at intermediate ratios MWW, FER, TON and MFI appear; at high ratios high-silica MFI, MTW, *BEA and BEC dominate; extreme ratios in the absence of mineralizer/OSDA increase the probability of Failed (amorphous or dense phases). Tree splits on this single descriptor should separate the label space along the low-silica / intermediate / high-silica axis far more sharply than splits on Si or Al alone.
descriptor.falsification: The descriptor is refuted if, in held-out publications, product framework is predicted as well by Si and Al as separate columns as by the ratio (i.e. the added column does not change split behaviour), or if syntheses with identical gel Si/Al but different framework outcomes show no systematic enrichment along the ratio axis (e.g. FAU and *BEA obtained at statistically indistinguishable Si/Al), or if the ratio systematically misleads in aluminophosphate recipes where Al is high but the determinant is P/Al rather than Si/Al.
descriptor.hypothesis: The gel silicon-to-aluminium ratio is the primary compositional variable steering framework selection: low ratios (Al-rich, alkali-rich gels) favour low-silica frameworks (FAU, LTA, SOD, MOR, zeolite A-type phases), intermediate-to-high ratios favour medium- and high-silica frameworks (MFI, TON, FER, MTW, MWW), and very high ratios, especially in fluoride or OSDA-dominated media, favour high-silica *BEA-type and pure-silica phases. Because Si and Al enter the classifier only as separate normalized mole fractions of a gel that also contains water, OSDA and OH, a tree ensemble splitting on one column at a time cannot directly express their ratio; the same Si mole fraction at 10x different Al level lands in different leaves even though the Si/Al chemistry is identical. Encoding the ratio explicitly makes this discriminating axis directly splittable and, being a dimensionless compositional quantity, transfers to recipes from unseen papers far better than absolute gel concentrations.
descriptor.mechanism: Framework topology fixes the framework Al content through Löwenstein-type constraints and charge balance: each framework-framework Al requires a charge-compensating cation (Na, K, TMA, etc.) or an OSDA proton. The achievable framework Si/Al is thus bounded by the gel Si/Al, and each zeolite phase occupies a characteristic Si/Al window (e.g. FAU and LTA crystallize at Si/Al roughly 1-5, MOR at ~5-20, MFI across ~10 to essentially pure silica, *BEA typically >10, aluminophosphates like AFI/AEL/AEI at Al/Si near infinity when P substitutes for Si). Crystallization is autoselective: nucleation of a phase is fastest where the gel can supply its characteristic Si/Al without large compositional gradients, so gel Si/Al acts as a thermodynamic prior on which framework nucleates first. The KG evidence is consistent with this: FAU and LTA experiments are overwhelmingly alkali-mediated low-temperature syntheses (median 90-100 C, fluoride in only 1-3%) typical of low-silica gels [1][2], whereas MFI (median 160 C) and especially *BEA (25% fluoride medium, Ge/Sn/Ti heteroatom-rich) are typical of high-silica, fluoride/OSDA-dominated media [3][4].

queries: OH/Si alkalinity ranges for fluoride-mediated beta BEC UTL syntheses vs hydroxide MFI FAU
plan.why: Alkalinity is the second canonical synthesis variable after Si/Al: it sets the rate of silica dissolution, nucleation density, and the trade-off between thermodynamic stability and kinetic accessibility. High alkalinity (>~0.1 OH/Si) drives low-silica, alkali-templated phases (FAU, LTA, SOD, zeolite P) and accelerates crystallization toward dense alkali silicates (Failed), while low alkalinity (especially near-neutral fluoride media or OSDA-dominated gels) suppresses nucleation and favours high-silica, defect-free frameworks (*BEA, MFI, MTW, BEC, UTL) that often crystallize only in narrow alkalinity windows. The classifier receives OH and Si only as separate normalized mole fractions of a gel whose other components (water, OSDA, heteroatoms) vary by orders of magnitude across publications, so splitting on either column alone cannot express the ratio: the same OH mole fraction at 10x different Si content is chemically a 10x change in alkalinity but lands in the same leaf. A tree ensemble can only approximate this ratio through many coordinated splits, which it rarely learns; encoding OH/(Si+0.001) explicitly makes this dimensionless, transferable axis directly splittable, complementing the already-appended Si/Al descriptor without duplicating it.

descriptor.assumptions: OH mole fraction is taken as total alkalinity, ignoring that OH is partly consumed by neutralization of the OSDA charge, by H+ from acid sources, and that fluoride gels may contain little free OH even when OH is recorded as a compensating cation amount; alkalinity per Si is only a proxy for true solution pH, which also depends on water content and counter-cations (Na, K). The 0.001 constant protects against Si=0 gels (e.g. aluminophosphate syntheses like AFI/AEL, where alkalinity per Si is meaningless and the feature saturates at very large values, which trees can isolate as their own region). Not a monotone transform of any single D0 column since it combines OH and Si.
descriptor.expected_effect: As gel_oh_si_ratio increases from ~0 to very large values (note: since OH is a normalized mole fraction, the ratio spans orders of magnitude; trees handle this wide range via log-like splits on the raw value), outcomes should shift from high-silica OSDA-templated frameworks (*BEA, BEC, UTL, MTW, MFI-silicalite-type) at low values, through intermediate phases (MFI, MWW, TON, FER) at moderate values, to low-silica alkali frameworks (FAU, LTA, MOR, SOD-type) at high values, with very high alkalinity increasing the Failed rate (dense alkali silicates / amorphous collapse).
descriptor.falsification: If held-out predictions do not improve and tree importances for this feature stay near zero after adding it on top of gel_si_al_ratio, or if the empirically observed ordering of frameworks along OH/Si contradicts the expected low-alkalinity -> high-silica/*BEA-family and high-alkalinity -> FAU/LTA/Failed trend (e.g. low-silica frameworks dominating at OH/Si < 0.05 or high-silica *BEA/BEC/UTL dominating at OH/Si > 1), the hypothesis is falsified. Also falsified if the feature merely duplicates splits already achieved via OH alone.
descriptor.hypothesis: Gel alkalinity, expressed as the OH-to-Si molar ratio, is the second canonical compositional variable steering framework selection after Si/Al. Low alkalinity (OH/Si near or below ~0.05, typical of fluoride-mediated or OSDA-dominated near-neutral gels) slows silicate dissolution and suppresses homogeneous nucleation, favouring high-silica, defect-free frameworks such as *BEA, BEC, UTL, MTW and MFI that crystallize only in narrow alkalinity windows; high alkalinity (OH/Si above ~0.1-0.5) accelerates dissolution and nucleation, driving low-silica, alkali-templated frameworks (FAU, LTA, SOD-type P phases) and, at extreme values, dense alkali silicates (Failed). Because OH and Si enter the classifier only as separate normalized mole fractions of a gel whose water, OSDA and heteroatom content varies by orders of magnitude across publications, a tree ensemble splitting on one column at a time cannot directly express this ratio: the same OH mole fraction at 10x different Si level is chemically a 10x alkalinity change but lands in the same leaf.
descriptor.mechanism: Hydroxide concentration per framework-forming tetrahedral atom (here proxied per Si) controls the depolymerization rate of the silica/aluminosilicate source, the concentration of soluble anionic silicate oligomers, and hence supersaturation and nucleation density. High OH/Si keeps silicate dissolved as monomers and small oligomers, favours low framework densities and alkali charge-balancing of Al, and speeds kinetic crystallization of open low-silica frameworks or amorphous/dense side phases. Low OH/Si (often with F- replacing OH- as mineralizer and/or a bulky OSDA dominating charge balance) yields slowly equilibrating, near-neutral gels where large, highly siliceous frameworks with strained 4-membered rings (*BEA, BEC, UTL) nucleate preferentially. The KG shows this axis covaries with phase selection: fluoride/near-neutral media (the low-OH regime) produce mostly *BEA, MFI and other medium-to-large-pore high-silica frameworks with *BEA at 25% of fluoride-mediated outcomes (item 6), and the framework-level data place high-silica Germanosilicate UTL and BEC and *BEA at higher median temperatures (170-175 C, items 2, 5) consistent with sluggish low-alkalinity crystallization, whereas FAU (all but 1% hydroxide media, median 100 C, item 3) crystallizes fast in strongly alkaline gels.

plan.factor: Gel dilution: water-to-(Si+Al+P) molar ratio (crystallization solvent loading)
queries: frameworks obtained in dilute vs concentrated gels (water-to-silica ratio) for MFI and *BEA
fluoride-mediated high-silica zeolite syntheses typical water/framework-mole ratios
plan.why: Water content is the third canonical gel variable after Si/Al and alkalinity, and the KG contains no gel-ratio information, so it is untouched by prior rounds. Dilution controls supersaturation and thus nucleation rate and crystal-size regime: concentrated (low-H2O) gels nucleate rapidly and favour dense/small-pore, alkali-rich phases (LTA, SOD, GIS, ANA, or Failed amorphous/dense products), whereas dilute gels slow nucleation and favour well-resolved open frameworks and large crystals (*BEA, MFI, MTW, MWW, AFI); fluoride-mediated high-silica syntheses are typically very dilute (H2O/TMI tens to hundreds), while inorganic low-silica syntheses are concentrated. Water enters the classifier only as one normalized mole fraction summed with all other species, so the same H2O mole fraction means a ~10x different H2O/Si ratio depending on the other components: a tree ensemble splitting on one column cannot express this ratio, and an absolute H2O value transfers poorly across papers with different normalization conventions. A dimensionless H2O/(Si+Al+P) ratio makes this discriminating axis directly splittable and robust to unseen-paper normalization differences.

descriptor.assumptions: The formula assumes H2O mole fraction reflects the actual synthesis dilution (i.e. measured/charged water, not water of crystallization lost in drying) and that Si+Al+P is an adequate proxy for the framework-forming solute loading; it ignores B, Ge, Ga, Ti and other heteroatoms that also form frameworks, and it treats water as inert (it also participates as a mineralizing agent and structure-directing hydration shell, which the ratio does not capture). Papers that quote water separately from the normalized gel are approximated by the normalized fraction; the +0.001 constant only guards against division by zero for essentially water-free systems.
descriptor.expected_effect: As gel_h2o_framework_ratio increases, the model should shift predictions from Failed, dense/small-pore alkali phases (LTA, SOD, GIS, ANA) toward open large- and medium-pore frameworks (MFI, *BEA, MTW, MWW, AFI, CHA, UTL, BEC), especially at high Si/Al and low OH/Si where the previously appended descriptors already indicate high-silica conditions; the combination high Si/Al, low OH/Si, high H2O/(Si+Al+P) should strongly favour *BEA and MFI, consistent with their prevalence in dilute fluoride media [1, 3].
descriptor.falsification: If product phase is in practice invariant to H2O/(Si+Al+P) once Si/Al and OH/Si are fixed (e.g. MFI and *BEA obtained across the full dilution range while LTA/Failed occur across all dilution levels within their compositional windows), or if the raw H2O mole fraction alone already captures all split-relevant variation so the ratio adds no separations, the descriptor should contribute no accuracy and the hypothesis is falsified.
descriptor.hypothesis: The water-to-framework-forming-element ratio (H2O/(Si+Al+P)) is the third canonical gel variable after Si/Al and alkalinity, and steers product identity through its control of supersaturation and nucleation regime: concentrated gels (low ratio, typical of inorganic low-silica systems) drive fast homogeneous nucleation favouring dense, small-pore alkali-templated phases (LTA, SOD, GIS, ANA) or amorphous/dense Failed products, whereas dilute gels (high ratio) slow nucleation, favour fewer nuclei and larger crystals, and enable the well-resolved open frameworks obtained from OSDA- and fluoride-dominated media (MFI, *BEA, MTW, MWW, AFI, and the fluoride high-silica family). Because H2O enters the classifier only as one normalized mole fraction summed with all other species, the same H2O fraction corresponds to roughly an order-of-magnitude different H2O/Si depending on the other components, so a tree ensemble splitting one column at a time cannot express this ratio; an absolute H2O value also transfers poorly across publications with different normalization conventions, while the dimensionless ratio transfers to recipes from unseen papers.
descriptor.mechanism: Water dilutes the reactive silicate/alumino-phosphate species, setting the effective supersaturation at the crystallization temperature. At low H2O/T ratios the activity of dissolved framework-forming species is high, the nucleation barrier is crossed rapidly and abundantly, and metastable dense or small-pore phases (and gels that never resolve, i.e. Failed) dominate; at high H2O/T ratios dissolution and transport are slower, nucleation is sparse, and growth on a small number of OSDA- or heteroatom-directed nuclei yields open, high-porosity frameworks. Fluoride-mediated high-silica syntheses, which according to the evidence constitute 25% of *BEA preparations [1] and dominate fluoride-medium products together with MFI (*BEA 25%, MFI 21% of 318 fluoride experiments) [3], are conventionally run very dilute (H2O/SiO2 of tens to hundreds) to dissolve the fluoride mineralizer and slow nucleation, whereas alkali-rich inorganic gels are concentrated. The ratio is dimensionless and independent of how each paper normalizes its gel composition.
